area: Fracture clinic, outpatients, imaging, bone health and infection
question: What proportion of adults whose X-ray suggests possible bone sarcoma are given a suspected cancer pathway referral?
why: Bone sarcoma is rare but delay is common because the presenting X-ray is often first reported outside a cancer pathway (routine trauma or GP films); no audit of this referral step exists in the library.

standard.wording: Consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for adults if an X-ray suggests the possibility of bone sarcoma. [2015]

population: Inclusion: all adults (16 and over) whose plain X-ray report includes a comment raising the possibility of a bone tumour or sarcoma (e.g. 'cannot exclude', 'suspicious of', 'refer bone tumour service'), from any requesting source (GP, ED, fracture clinic, orthopaedics), over the last 12-24 months. Exclusion: known metastatic bone disease, known primary bone sarcoma already under follow-up.
sample: All eligible X-ray reports over the last 12-24 months (bone sarcoma referrals are rare; expect 5-15 cases per hospital, so pool radiology reporting system data across the trust or across a network if needed).
data_source: Radiology reporting system (text search for sarcoma/tumour/neoplasm terms in X-ray reports), 2-week wait referral log, PAS referral dates, and the bone sarcoma centre's referral inbox or letter.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-24 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory radiology 'critical result' alert that fires to the reporting radiologist's and requester's inbox whenever a bone tumour/sarcoma-suggestive phrase is used, with a same-day 2-week-wait referral form linked from the alert.
target: 100% (every suggestive report should trigger same-day referral)
reaudit: At 6 months, same case-finding method and time window
close_loop: Present at the radiology-orthopaedic governance meeting and trust cancer performance meeting; if the alert works, add the sarcoma-suggestive phrase list to the radiology reporting template's critical-results dictionary permanently.
evidence: No audit of bone sarcoma referral timeliness exists in the library (checked with query.py).
pitfalls: Numbers are tiny in a single hospital → pool data across a network or over 24 months, and report as 'x/y' not a percentage alone.
Free-text radiology reports make cases hard to find by search terms → agree the search phrase list with radiology before starting and screen a wider set manually.
Radiologists may already phone the referrer informally without a written referral → count a documented, dated phone call as a pass if a referral follows within 24 hours.
The finding may be an incidental old lesion (e.g. bone island) → have a second radiologist confirm true suspicion before including the case.
pearls: Recruit a musculoskeletal radiologist as co-lead; they can define the search terms and pull the report list.
Agree the definition of 'suggestive of sarcoma' before counting cases, using the regional bone sarcoma service's own referral criteria.
Link the audit to the regional bone sarcoma MDT's own referral log, which may already record delays.
Keep the critical-result alert switched on after the trainee rotates by naming a radiology governance lead as its owner.
effort: ~30 min per case (searching reports plus checking the referral log); expect only 5-15 cases so total effort is low
pass: A suspected cancer pathway (2-week wait) referral to a bone sarcoma service is made and documented on the day the report is authorised, or the same working day.

area: Fracture clinic, outpatients, imaging, bone health and infection
question: What proportion of children and young people whose X-ray suggests possible bone sarcoma get a specialist appointment within 48 hours?
why: NICE sets a tighter 48-hour standard for children than for adults because paediatric bone sarcomas grow faster; no audit of this step exists in the library, and the adult and paediatric pathways are often confused locally.

standard.source: NICE NG12 rec 1.11.2 (2015), with 'very urgent' defined in NG12 Terms used in this guideline
standard.wording: Consider a very urgent referral (for an appointment within 48 hours) for specialist assessment for children and young people if an X-ray suggests the possibility of bone sarcoma. [2015] ... Very urgent: To happen within 48 hours.

population: Inclusion: patients under 25 whose plain X-ray report raises the possibility of bone sarcoma, over the last 24-36 months (rare in children, so a long window is needed). Exclusion: known bone sarcoma already under follow-up.
sample: All eligible cases identified from the last 24-36 months of radiology reports across the network (expect very few cases in a single hospital; escalate to network level if under 5).
data_source: Radiology reporting system, referral log to the paediatric/teenage-and-young-adult bone sarcoma service, clinic letter or MDT record confirming the appointment date.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect (extended window for cases); Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-24 re-audit
change: Create a single 'child/young person: X-ray suggests bone sarcoma' escalation route that bypasses the general 2-week-wait office and goes straight to the on-call paediatric orthopaedic/oncology consultant by phone, logged on a shared tracker.
reaudit: At 12 months, same case-finding method
close_loop: Present at the paediatric orthopaedic and radiology governance meeting; if the direct escalation route works, publish it as a one-page pathway card kept in the radiology reporting room and the children's ED.
evidence: No audit of paediatric bone sarcoma referral timeliness exists in the library (checked with query.py).
pitfalls: Case numbers are very small → do not report a single percentage from under 5 cases; describe each case's timeline individually as well.
Out-of-hours reporting can delay the clock starting → record the time the report was authorised, not just the date.
Confusing the adult 2-week-wait pathway with the paediatric 48-hour pathway → make the escalation route unambiguous and age-based in the referral form.
Families may decline urgent transfer for practical reasons → record this separately, it is not a service failure.
pearls: Recruit the paediatric orthopaedic and paediatric oncology teams jointly, since the referral crosses both.
Use the regional bone sarcoma MDT's referral log as the second data source to catch cases the local search misses.
Fix the phone number and escalation script for the on-call route before cycle 1, not after the first missed case.
Keep the pathway card current by giving one named consultant ownership after the audit team rotates.
effort: ~30 min per case; case numbers are very low so total effort is small
pass: The child or young person (under 25) is seen by a bone sarcoma specialist (in person or virtually) within 48 hours of the X-ray report being authorised.

area: Fracture clinic, outpatients, imaging, bone health and infection
question: What proportion of children with unexplained bone swelling or pain get a direct access X-ray within 48 hours of the GP request?
why: NICE sets a 'very urgent' direct access X-ray standard for unexplained bone swelling or pain in children to catch bone sarcoma early; no audit of direct access imaging turnaround for this indication exists in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG12 rec 1.11.3 (2015), with 'very urgent' defined in NG12 Terms used in this guideline
standard.wording: Consider a very urgent, direct access X-ray to assess for bone sarcoma in children and young people with unexplained bone swelling or pain. [2015] ... Very urgent: To happen within 48 hours.

population: Inclusion: all direct access X-ray requests from primary care for children and young people (under 25) with the clinical details 'unexplained bone swelling' or 'unexplained bone pain', over the last 6-12 months. Exclusion: requests with an alternative clear cause given (e.g. recent injury, known infection).
sample: 30-40 consecutive eligible direct access requests over the last 6-12 months, from the radiology request system.
data_source: Radiology information system (RIS) request and performed dates/times for direct access paediatric X-rays with the relevant clinical details.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a RIS priority code for 'paediatric direct access - unexplained bone swelling/pain' that books automatically into the next available slot within 48 hours, separate from routine direct access X-ray priority.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the radiology and primary-care interface meeting; if the priority code reduces delay, keep it live in the RIS and tell local GP practices via the referral guidance intranet page.
evidence: No audit of direct access X-ray turnaround for suspected childhood bone sarcoma exists in the library (checked with query.py).
pitfalls: GP requests may not use the words 'unexplained' or specify duration → agree a pragmatic definition with radiology reception before starting.
School-age children may only attend after school or at weekends → check whether out-of-hours direct access slots exist locally.
Small numbers in a single practice's referrals → collect from radiology centrally rather than per-practice.
A slow report turnaround can hide a fast scan turnaround → measure scan date, not report date, against this standard.
pearls: Recruit a radiology superintendent radiographer to set up the priority code; they control RIS booking rules.
Share the finding with the local GP referral guidance so requesters know the 48-hour pathway exists.
Keep a running log of these referrals so the (rare) sarcoma-positive cases can be traced right through to specialist review.
Name a radiology governance lead to keep the priority code active after the audit team rotates.
effort: ~15 min per case from the RIS request log
pass: The X-ray is performed within 48 hours of the GP direct-access request being received by radiology.

question: What proportion of adults listed for ACL reconstruction are offered prehabilitation before surgery?
why: ACL reconstruction is one of the highest-volume knee soft-tissue operations in a DGH, but the library has no audit of the ACL-specific BOA/BASK-BOSTAA standard, only broader knee arthroscopy and problematic knee replacement audits (e.g. [ONA-090]).

standard.source: BOA Specialty Standard: Best Practice for Management of Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Injuries (September 2020), standard 3
standard.wording: All patients being considered for surgery should be offered prehabilitation to recover knee movement and quadriceps strength.

population: Inclusion: all adults listed for primary ACL reconstruction over the last 6-12 months. Exclusion: revision ACL surgery, multiligament reconstruction.
sample: 30-40 consecutive adults listed for primary ACL reconstruction over the last 6-12 months.
data_source: Knee/soft-tissue clinic letters, physiotherapy referral system, listing decision form in the EPR.

template.note: documented in pre-op assessment or op note

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic prehabilitation physiotherapy referral to the knee clinic listing form, triggered whenever 'ACL reconstruction' is selected as the planned procedure.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the knee/sports injury MDT or departmental audit meeting; if the automatic referral works, keep it as the default listing pathway for ACL reconstruction.
evidence: No audit of the BOA ACL standard exists in the library; only knee arthroscopy for osteoarthritis [ONA-090] and problematic knee replacement [ONA-095, ONA-096] are covered.
pitfalls: Patients seen privately or via self-referral physiotherapy before clinic may not have a hospital-documented referral → ask specifically and record patient-reported prehab too.
Some patients with an acutely locked knee proceed to urgent surgery without time for prehab → exclude or flag these separately rather than counting as a fail.
Physiotherapy waiting times may make 'offered' meaningless if never delivered → also record whether the patient attended at least one session before surgery.
Surgeons may assume prehab is 'standard practice' without checking it happened → make the referral itself, not the surgeon's assumption, the recorded evidence.
pearls: Recruit the knee/sports injury physiotherapist as co-lead; they can confirm attendance data.
Agree the definition of 'offered' (referral made, not just verbal advice) before cycle 1.
Use the knee clinic listing form as the single source of truth so the fix is easy to embed.
Keep the automatic referral live by naming the clinic's physiotherapy lead as its owner after rotation.
effort: ~15 min per patient from the clinic letter and physiotherapy referral system
pass: A documented referral to, or plan for, prehabilitation physiotherapy (range of movement and quadriceps strengthening) is recorded before the listing decision or at listing.

question: What proportion of adults having ACL reconstruction are registered on the National Ligament Registry?
why: Consent for, and registration on, the National Ligament Registry is a specific BOA standard for ACL surgery; the library's arthroplasty audits use the National Joint Registry but nothing audits ligament registry participation.

standard.source: BOA Specialty Standard: Best Practice for Management of Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Injuries (September 2020), standard 7d
standard.wording: Consent for inclusion into National Ligament Registry should be sought and patients should be registered in its database. Hospitals should facilitate the accurate recording of surgical procedures and patients' outcome by providing appropriate clerical and IT support.

population: Inclusion: all adults having primary ACL reconstruction over the last 6-12 months. Exclusion: none.
sample: 30-40 consecutive primary ACL reconstructions over the last 6-12 months.
data_source: Consent form, operation note, National Ligament Registry local upload log or export.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'Ligament Registry consent: yes/no/declined' field to the ACL operation note template that cannot be saved blank, linked to an automatic upload task for theatre administrative staff.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the knee/sports injury MDT; if the mandatory field improves capture, keep it in the operation note template and give the registry upload task a named owner.
evidence: No audit of National Ligament Registry participation exists in the library; National Joint Registry participation is a separate, unaudited topic too.
pitfalls: Staff may confuse the National Ligament Registry with the National Joint Registry → clarify which registry is being audited in the template and this protocol.
Registration can lag behind surgery by weeks → measure both consent documentation and eventual upload, not just one.
Patients may decline consent → record this as a valid reason, not a failure, but still count it in the denominator.
IT or clerical understaffing may be the real bottleneck → escalate this as a service gap if the fix does not work, per the standard's own wording.
pearls: Recruit the theatre coordinator or department secretary who manages registry uploads as co-lead.
Check the registry's own dashboard for the unit's baseline capture rate before cycle 1 if it already exists.
Make the consent conversation part of the standard ACL consent script so it is never missed.
Name a registry data lead to keep uploads current after the audit team rotates.
effort: ~10 min per patient from the consent form and registry log
pass: Consent for the National Ligament Registry is documented on the consent form or in the notes, and the case is found on the registry's local upload log.

question: What proportion of ACL reconstruction operation notes document the examination under anaesthesia findings?
why: The BOA ACL standard requires a documented EUA of anteroposterior and rotational laxity and associated injuries at every reconstruction; this specific documentation item is not covered by any audit in the library.

standard.source: BOA Specialty Standard: Best Practice for Management of Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Injuries (September 2020), standard 8d
standard.wording: An examination under anaesthetic must be performed to take into account the degree of anteroposterior and rotational laxity as well as any other associated injuries and documented.

population: Inclusion: all adults having primary or revision ACL reconstruction over the last 3-6 months. Exclusion: none.
sample: 30-40 consecutive ACL reconstruction operation notes over the last 3-6 months.
data_source: Operation note in the EPR or paper theatre record.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory structured EUA section (AP laxity, pivot shift/rotational laxity, other injuries) to the ACL operation note template that must be completed before the note can be saved.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the knee/sports injury MDT; if the structured field improves documentation, keep it as the standard ACL operation note template.
evidence: No audit of EUA documentation completeness for ACL reconstruction exists in the library.
pitfalls: Free-text operation notes may describe the EUA in prose without clearly separating each element → agree what counts as 'documented' before starting (all three elements named, even briefly).
Trainees may perform and record the EUA differently from consultants → record operator grade to see if this varies.
A dictated note may be transcribed late, after the data collection window → check for addenda before marking a case a fail.
The fix only works if surgeons actually complete the structured field rather than leaving it blank → spot-check a sample after go-live.
pearls: Recruit a knee surgery registrar to help design the structured field wording with the consultants.
Pilot the template on one theatre list before rolling it out trust-wide.
Use real anonymised examples of good and poor documentation in teaching to fix the standard quickly.
Keep the field mandatory (not just present) so it survives staff turnover.
effort: ~10 min per operation note
pass: The operation note records EUA findings for anteroposterior laxity, rotational (pivot shift) laxity, and any other associated injury found.

question: What proportion of patients cleared to return to sport after ACL reconstruction have criteria-based testing documented?
why: The BOA ACL standard requires criteria-based (not time-based alone) return-to-sport testing including strength and hop tests; no audit of this final rehabilitation milestone exists in the library, which otherwise stops at the operative standards.

standard.source: BOA Specialty Standard: Best Practice for Management of Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Injuries (September 2020), standard 10
standard.wording: Decision to return to sport should be criteria based taking into consideration physical factors relating to the knee; psychological factors including fear of reinjury and social factors; while being tailored to the specific sport. To assess readiness to return to play and the risk for reinjury, a range of tests, including strength tests, hop tests and measurement of movement quality, should be used.

population: Inclusion: all adults discharged from physiotherapy with return-to-sport clearance after primary ACL reconstruction, over the last 12 months. Exclusion: patients who did not return to sport or were discharged for other reasons.
sample: 30 consecutive return-to-sport discharges over the last 12 months (this milestone occurs 9-12 months post-surgery, so a longer window is needed).
data_source: Physiotherapy discharge letter or return-to-sport assessment record.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce a standard 'ACL return-to-sport testing battery' form (quadriceps/hamstring strength ratio, single-leg hop tests, psychological readiness scale) that must be completed and filed before a return-to-sport letter is issued.
reaudit: At 12 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the physiotherapy and knee/sports injury MDT joint meeting; if the testing battery is adopted, embed it in the physiotherapy department's standard operating procedure.
evidence: No audit of criteria-based return-to-sport testing after ACL reconstruction exists in the library.
pitfalls: Return-to-sport decisions may be made informally by the patient without a final physiotherapy discharge letter → agree with physiotherapy how these are captured before starting.
Testing equipment (hop test space, dynamometer) may not be available in every clinic → note equipment gaps as a barrier, not just a documentation failure.
Patients may return to sport gradually with no single 'clearance' event → allow a range of dates and pick the first formal sign-off.
Sport-specific tailoring (e.g. football versus running) can make a single checklist feel rigid → keep the form flexible with a sport-specific notes field.
pearls: Recruit the lead sports physiotherapist to design and own the testing battery.
Benchmark against the local ACL rehabilitation pathway if one already exists informally.
Share results with patients as part of their own rehabilitation goal-setting; it increases engagement with testing.
Keep the form in the physiotherapy department's shared drive so it outlives individual staff rotations.
effort: ~15 min per patient from the physiotherapy discharge record
pass: The physiotherapy discharge or return-to-sport letter records at least one strength test and one hop test result supporting the return-to-sport decision, not a time-since-surgery statement alone.

question: What proportion of adults assessed for recurrent patellar instability have all the required MRI findings documented?
why: A separate BOA/BASK specialty standard sets out the specific MRI findings needed before surgical decision-making for recurrent patellar instability; the library's only patellar-dislocation audit [ONA-166] covers the very different first-time-dislocation X-ray standard.

standard.source: BOA Specialty Standard: The Assessment of Patients with Recurrent Patellar Instability (August 2020), standards 3 and 5
standard.wording: Further imaging investigations should include an MRI of the knee (unless MRI contra-indicated) which includes axial and sagittal images. The MRI aims to outline: Patella alta ...; Degenerative change or cartilage loss; Loose osteochondral or chondral fragment; Meniscal and ligamentous pathology; Trochlear dysplasia; Tibial tuberosity offset. ... Determination of patella alta involves assessment of the clinical picture and radiological imaging, and may include indices such as patellotrochlear overlap, Caton-Dechamps ratio or Blackburne-Peel ratio according to published normal ranges.

population: Inclusion: adults with recurrent (two or more) patellar dislocations having an MRI as part of surgical work-up, over the last 12 months. Exclusion: first-time dislocation, patients with significant knee degenerative change managed non-operatively.
sample: 30 consecutive recurrent patellar instability MRI work-ups over the last 12 months.
data_source: MRI report and knee/soft-tissue clinic letter.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Create a structured MRI reporting proforma for 'recurrent patellar instability' in the radiology system that prompts the reporting radiologist for each of the three required measurements.
reaudit: At 4-6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the joint knee-radiology MDT; if the proforma improves completeness, keep it as the default template for this MRI indication.
evidence: No audit of MRI reporting completeness for recurrent patellar instability exists in the library; the only patellar-dislocation audit [ONA-166] covers first-time-dislocation X-rays instead.
pitfalls: Non-specialist radiologists reporting out of hours may not know the required measurements → target the proforma fix at general as well as MSK radiology.
Different named indices (Caton-Deschamps versus Blackburne-Peel) may be used interchangeably → accept any recognised index as a pass.
Requesting clinicians may not specify 'recurrent patellar instability' on the request, making cases hard to find → agree a standard request wording with the knee clinic first.
Adding fields to the proforma can slow reporting turnaround → monitor report turnaround time alongside completeness.
pearls: Recruit the MSK radiology lead as co-lead; the proforma change is theirs to make.
Use example reports from the current baseline to show radiology colleagues exactly what is missing.
Link the proforma to the knee clinic's surgical decision-making template so surgeons flag if a needed measurement is absent.
Keep the proforma live by adding it to radiology's standard reporting templates list, not a personal favourite.
effort: ~10 min per MRI report
pass: The MRI report or clinic letter documents a comment on patella height (an index such as Caton-Deschamps or Blackburne-Peel or 'patella alta: yes/no'), trochlear morphology, and tibial tuberosity offset, for a patient being worked up for recurrent patellar instability surgery.

question: What proportion of adults having arthroscopic meniscal surgery have a preoperative MRI confirming a meniscal lesion?
why: The national BASK meniscal guideline states the flowchart only applies once MRI confirms a lesion, but the library's only knee arthroscopy audit [ONA-090] covers mechanical locking in osteoarthritis, not MRI confirmation for meniscal surgery generally.

standard.source: BASK Arthroscopic Meniscal Surgery: A National Society Treatment Guideline and Consensus Statement (Bone Joint J 2019;101-B:652-659)
standard.wording: It was agreed that for the guidance from the flowchart to be applicable, MRI confirmation of a lesion would be necessary.

population: Inclusion: all adults having elective arthroscopic partial meniscectomy or meniscal repair over the last 3-6 months. Exclusion: acute locked knee proceeding to emergency arthroscopy without preoperative MRI, combined ACL reconstruction cases (covered separately).
sample: 40 consecutive elective arthroscopic meniscal surgery cases over the last 3-6 months.
data_source: Theatre list/operation note, MRI report, pre-listing clinic letter.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'MRI target confirmed: yes, side/compartment ___' field to the elective knee arthroscopy listing form, which must be completed before the case can be added to a theatre list.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the knee/sports injury MDT or departmental audit meeting; if the mandatory field works, keep it in the listing form permanently.
evidence: No audit of MRI confirmation before elective meniscal surgery exists in the library; [ONA-090] covers a different indication (mechanical locking in osteoarthritis).
pitfalls: Surgeons occasionally proceed on clinical grounds alone in a clear-cut case → record and discuss these as a deliberate exception, not simply a fail.
MRI and clinical side/compartment can be transcribed incorrectly between systems → cross-check the operation note against the MRI report directly, not just clinic letters.
Waiting times for MRI may create pressure to list before the scan is back → escalate this as a capacity issue if it appears repeatedly.
'Possible target' lesions are a genuine grey area in the guideline → record separately from clear 'target' lesions rather than combining them.
pearls: Recruit the knee/sports injury lead surgeon to define what counts as a 'target' lesion for local use.
Check MRI waiting times before cycle 1; a listing delay is often the true bottleneck, not documentation.
Present findings by individual surgeon (anonymised) to encourage engagement without blame.
Keep the mandatory field in place after rotation by embedding it in the department's standard listing proforma.
effort: ~15 min per case from the MRI report and listing form
pass: An MRI report before surgery describes a meniscal 'target' or 'possible target' lesion matching the side and compartment operated on (locked knee cases needing emergency surgery before MRI is possible are excluded, per the guideline).

question: What proportion of adults with a locked knee from a meniscal tear have urgent arthroscopic surgery documented as planned within the recommended timeframe?
why: The BASK meniscal guideline classifies a locked knee as needing urgent arthroscopic surgery, distinct from routine meniscal tear management; no audit in the library measures how quickly locked knees reach theatre.

standard.source: BASK Arthroscopic Meniscal Surgery: A National Society Treatment Guideline and Consensus Statement (Bone Joint J 2019;101-B:652-659), Meniscal Tear Management Guideline flowchart
standard.wording: Locked Knee: Assessment: Arthroscopic meniscal surgery indicated. Recommendation: Urgent Arthroscopic Meniscal Surgery.

population: Inclusion: adults presenting with a clinically locked knee (unable to fully extend) attributed to a meniscal tear, over the last 6-12 months. Exclusion: locking due to loose body from other pathology, pre-existing severe osteoarthritis.
sample: 20-30 consecutive locked knee presentations over the last 6-12 months (locked knee is less common than routine meniscal referrals, so a longer window may be needed).
data_source: ED/clinic assessment note, theatre booking system, operation note.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add 'locked knee (meniscal)' as a named category on the trauma/urgent theatre booking form with a 7-day target, so it is not booked onto a routine elective waiting list.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the knee/sports injury and trauma theatre governance meeting; if the booking category works, keep it as a standing theatre priority category.
evidence: No audit of locked-knee-to-surgery timing for meniscal tears exists in the library.
pitfalls: Locked knee can be misdiagnosed as simple knee pain and missed from case-finding → search ED and clinic coding broadly, not just theatre lists.
Elective and trauma theatre capacity may compete for the same slots → present findings alongside theatre capacity data, not in isolation.
A knee that 'unlocks' spontaneously before surgery may no longer need urgent listing → record this as a valid change of plan, not a fail.
Different clinicians may disagree on what counts as 'locked' → agree a clinical definition (fixed flexion deformity, unable to fully extend) before starting.
pearls: Recruit the trauma coordinator to help identify locked knee cases from the daily trauma list.
Agree the 7-day target and definition of 'locked' with the knee/sports injury lead before cycle 1.
Track whether the urgent booking category is actually used, not just whether it exists, at re-audit.
Keep the category live in the booking system by naming a trauma coordinator as its permanent owner.
effort: ~15 min per case from the assessment note and theatre system
pass: Surgery is performed within 7 days of the locked knee being diagnosed by the knee/orthopaedic team, or a documented clinical reason for a longer wait is recorded.

question: What proportion of adults with advanced knee osteoarthritis and a meniscal tear on MRI are correctly NOT listed for arthroscopic meniscal surgery?
why: The BASK guideline explicitly advises against meniscal surgery in advanced structural osteoarthritis; the library's AoMRC Evidence-Based Interventions audit [ONA-090] checks for a history of true locking but does not check this specific overuse scenario.

standard.source: BASK Arthroscopic Meniscal Surgery: A National Society Treatment Guideline and Consensus Statement (Bone Joint J 2019;101-B:652-659), Meniscal Tear Management Guideline flowchart
standard.wording: Advanced Structural OA & Meniscal Tear (or Arthritic Symptoms/Signs only). Assessment: Arthroscopic meniscal surgery usually* not appropriate. Recommendation: No Arthroscopic Meniscal Surgery (Provide information and consider physiotherapy, exercise, analgesia, weight loss, steroid injection, arthroplasty). *Except in uncommon special cases (a second opinion is advised).

population: Inclusion: adults with a knee MRI showing both advanced structural osteoarthritis and a meniscal tear, discussed in a knee clinic over the last 12 months. Exclusion: locked knee, mild or no osteoarthritis with a meniscal tear (covered by [ONA-090] and other pathways).
sample: 30 consecutive knee clinic patients with MRI-confirmed advanced OA and a meniscal tear over the last 12 months.
data_source: MRI report, knee clinic letter, theatre booking system.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 'BASK advanced OA + meniscal tear' prompt to the knee clinic letter template that appears when advanced OA is coded, requiring either a non-operative plan or a documented second-opinion reason for surgery.
target: ≥90% managed non-operatively (or with documented second opinion)
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the knee/sports injury MDT and evidence-based intervention governance meeting; if the prompt reduces inappropriate listings, keep it in the clinic letter template.
evidence: No audit of this specific BASK overuse scenario exists in the library; [ONA-090] audits a different criterion (mechanical locking) for a different AoMRC standard.
pitfalls: Grading osteoarthritis severity consistently between clinicians is difficult → agree a simple local definition (e.g. Kellgren-Lawrence 3-4, or 'bone-on-bone' on MRI/X-ray) before starting.
Surgeons may list for a genuine uncommon exception without documenting a second opinion → make the second-opinion box explicit and easy to complete.
Patients may push for surgery having read about it online → record shared decision-making discussion as part of the non-operative pathway.
This can feel like scrutiny of individual surgeons' listing decisions → present anonymised, aggregate data first.
pearls: Recruit the knee clinic lead and a second senior colleague to define the local osteoarthritis severity threshold.
Link the audit to existing AoMRC Evidence-Based Interventions governance processes already used for [ONA-090], since the listing form may already exist.
Share the evidence base (BASK guideline) directly with the surgical team before presenting results, to pre-empt disagreement.
Keep the clinic letter prompt live by adding it to the standard knee clinic template, not a personal one.
effort: ~15 min per case from the MRI report and clinic letter
pass: A patient with advanced structural osteoarthritis (Kellgren-Lawrence grade 3-4 or equivalent MRI cartilage loss) and a meniscal tear on MRI is managed non-operatively (physiotherapy, weight, analgesia, injection or arthroplasty pathway), or a documented second opinion supports the uncommon exception.

question: What proportion of primary ACL reconstructions are performed as a day case?
why: The BOA ACL standard states the procedure should be a day case for most patients, which affects both patient experience and bed capacity, but no audit of day-case rates for ACL reconstruction exists in the library.

standard.source: BOA Specialty Standard: Best Practice for Management of Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Injuries (September 2020), standard 8a
standard.wording: The procedure should be performed on a Day Case basis, for majority of patients. The surgery should be performed by or under supervision of a surgeon with special interest in soft tissue knee reconstruction.

population: Inclusion: all adults having primary ACL reconstruction over the last 6-12 months. Exclusion: combined multiligament reconstruction, revision surgery.
sample: 40 consecutive primary ACL reconstructions over the last 6-12 months.
data_source: Theatre system admission and discharge dates, ward discharge summary.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Move routine primary ACL reconstruction onto a dedicated day-case theatre list with a morning start time, a standard multimodal analgesia and nerve block protocol, and a same-day physiotherapy discharge checklist.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the knee/sports injury MDT and day-case governance meeting; if the dedicated list improves the day-case rate, make it the standing list model.
evidence: No audit of ACL reconstruction day-case rates exists in the library.
pitfalls: Afternoon list starts make same-day discharge harder → record list start time to see if this explains variation.
Patients travelling a long distance or living alone may need to stay for social reasons → record these as valid reasons, not failures.
Combined meniscal repair or associated injuries can extend recovery time → note any additional procedure performed at the same sitting.
A push to hit the day-case target could discharge patients before pain and mobility are safe → monitor unplanned re-attendance rates alongside the day-case rate.
pearls: Recruit the day-case unit manager and the anaesthetic lead, since analgesia and list timing drive the outcome.
Agree the standard analgesia and nerve block protocol with anaesthetics before cycle 1.
Check readmission or unplanned contact rates at re-audit to confirm the change is safe, not just efficient.
Keep the dedicated list running by giving the day-case unit ownership of the booking template after rotation.
effort: ~10 min per case from the theatre and ward systems
pass: The patient is admitted and discharged on the same calendar day as surgery, with no overnight stay, unless a documented medical or social reason justifies admission.

question: What proportion of patients with an open fracture receive intravenous antibiotics within 1 hour of injury?
why: Timely antibiotics are the single most evidence-based intervention for reducing infection after open fracture, but the library has no audit of this specific timing standard; existing open-fracture and fracture-related-infection audits [ONA-141] focus on sampling, not the initial antibiotic clock.

standard.source: BOA/BAPRAS Audit Standards for Trauma: Open Fractures (December 2017), standard 2
standard.wording: Intravenous prophylactic antibiotics should be administered as soon as possible, ideally within 1 hour of injury.

population: Inclusion: all patients with an open fracture of a long bone, hindfoot or midfoot presenting to the emergency department over the last 3 months. Exclusion: hand, wrist, forefoot or digit injuries (managed under a different principle per the standard), patients who received pre-hospital antibiotics (record separately).
sample: 40 consecutive open fracture presentations over the last 3-6 months.
data_source: Ambulance patient report form (for injury/pre-hospital antibiotic time), ED drug chart or e-prescribing record, ED triage record.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add open fracture antibiotics to the ED trauma triage 'time-critical medicine' checklist with a pre-drawn-up antibiotic kept in the resus and majors antibiotic cupboard, triggered by the trauma call or open fracture triage category.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the trauma network open fracture governance meeting and submit alongside routine TARN data; if the checklist works, add it permanently to the trauma triage proforma.
evidence: No audit of the 1-hour open fracture antibiotic standard exists in the library; the related fracture-related-infection audit [ONA-141] measures microbiology sampling, not antibiotic timing.
pitfalls: Injury time is often an estimate, especially for unwitnessed or intoxicated patients → record the source of the time and analyse both scenarios.
Pre-hospital antibiotics given by ambulance crews may not be visible in the hospital drug chart → check the ambulance record specifically.
A polytrauma patient may have antibiotics delayed by resuscitation priorities → record this as a clinical reason, not simply a fail, but still report it.
'As soon as possible' can be read as more lenient than 'within 1 hour' → use the 1-hour figure as the audited pass criterion, consistent with the standard's own wording.
pearls: Recruit an ED trauma nurse coordinator; they can identify open fracture attendances quickly from the trauma call log.
Pre-draw antibiotics for common open fracture protocols so the drug itself is never the delay.
Present results alongside the trust's TARN open fracture data, which may already flag delays.
Keep the checklist item live by linking it to the trauma call proforma rather than a stand-alone poster.
effort: ~15 min per patient from the ED and ambulance records
pass: IV prophylactic antibiotics are given within 1 hour of the recorded time of injury (or time of arrival if injury time is unknown, documented as such).

question: What proportion of open fracture wounds are photographed before debridement?
why: The BOA/BAPRAS open fracture standard requires photography of the wound before debridement to reduce repeated dressing changes and support the orthoplastic decision, but no audit of photography compliance exists in the library.

standard.source: BOA/BAPRAS Audit Standards for Trauma: Open Fractures (December 2017), standards 9 and 10
standard.wording: Photographs of open fracture wounds should be taken when they are first exposed for clinical care, before debridement and at other key stages of management. These should be kept in the patient's records.

population: Inclusion: all patients with an open fracture of a long bone, hindfoot or midfoot over the last 3 months. Exclusion: hand, wrist, forefoot or digit injuries.
sample: 40 consecutive open fracture presentations over the last 3-6 months.
data_source: Clinical photography system, ED and orthopaedic clerking notes.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Issue a dedicated, information-governance-approved clinical photography device in ED resus/majors with a direct upload link to the EPR, and add 'wound photographed: yes/no' to the open fracture ED proforma.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the trauma network open fracture governance meeting; if the dedicated device and proforma field improve compliance, keep both as standard ED trauma equipment.
evidence: No audit of open fracture wound photography exists in the library.
pitfalls: Staff may take photographs on personal phones due to convenience, breaching information governance → the fix must make the approved device easier to use than the alternative.
Photographs taken but not properly filed or linked to the right patient are effectively a fail → check the record, not just staff recollection.
Photography can be delayed by resuscitation priorities in a polytrauma patient → record this as a reason, not simply omit the case.
Repeated exposure of the wound to reposition for photography risks contamination → the standard specifically asks for photography at first exposure, so time this carefully.
pearls: Recruit the ED trauma lead and the trust's information governance team early, since device approval is the main barrier.
Site the approved device somewhere staff will actually reach for it (resus wall mount, on the trauma trolley).
Use the photograph itself in trauma meeting teaching to reinforce the value of early photography.
Keep the device stocked and working by giving ED equipment services ownership after the audit team rotates.
effort: ~10 min per patient from the ED notes and photography system
pass: At least one photograph of the open fracture wound taken before debridement is filed in the patient's clinical record (EPR clinical photography system or equivalent).

area: Fracture clinic, outpatients, imaging, bone health and infection
question: What proportion of inpatients with proven or suspected fracture-related infection are discussed at a weekly bone and joint infection MDT?
why: The BOAST Fracture Related Infections standard requires weekly MDT review of these inpatients to rationalise surgical and antimicrobial management; the library's only FRI audits [ONA-141, ONA-037, ONA-038] cover sampling and consultant review, not ongoing MDT oversight.

standard.source: BOAST Fracture Related Infections (September 2019), standard 7B
standard.wording: All in-patients with proven or suspected FRI should be the subject of weekly bone and joint infection MDT review to rationalise surgical strategy and antimicrobial management. MDT time should be sufficient to review relevant out-patients too.

population: Inclusion: all inpatients with a diagnosis of proven or suspected fracture-related infection over the last 3-6 months. Exclusion: patients discharged within 7 days of diagnosis (no full week to audit).
sample: 20-30 consecutive inpatient episodes with proven or suspected FRI over the last 3-6 months.
data_source: MDT minutes or outcome log, inpatient notes, microbiology/infection team records.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Create a standing weekly bone and joint infection MDT with a running inpatient tracker list (populated automatically from the microbiology alert system) so no FRI inpatient can be missed from the agenda.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the orthopaedic infection governance meeting; if the tracker list works, hand ownership to the infection MDT coordinator as a permanent process.
evidence: No audit of weekly bone and joint infection MDT review exists in the library; [ONA-141] covers sampling and [ONA-037]/[ONA-038] cover the initial consultant review and GP advice, not ongoing MDT oversight.
pitfalls: If no formal bone and joint infection MDT exists locally, this audit will show 0% and should prompt setting one up rather than just documenting the gap → say so plainly in the report.
MDT discussion may happen informally on the ward round without being logged → agree that only a dated, attributable record counts as a pass.
Patients transferred between wards or hospitals mid-treatment are easy to lose from the tracker → cross-check against the microbiology alert list weekly.
A weekly MDT can become tokenistic if only 'discussed, no change' is recorded → also capture whether an actual management decision was documented.
pearls: Recruit a consultant microbiologist or infectious diseases physician as co-lead; the MDT needs their commitment to be sustainable.
Use the existing FRI sampling audit process [ONA-141] as the case-finding route for this audit too, since the same patients are involved.
Agree MDT membership and a fixed weekly slot before cycle 1, not after gaps appear.
Keep the MDT running after rotation by giving it a standing slot in the theatre/clinic timetable, not an ad hoc booking.
effort: ~20 min per patient episode cross-checking MDT records against the notes
pass: Every full week of the inpatient stay with proven or suspected FRI has a documented bone and joint infection MDT discussion (attendance list and outcome recorded).

area: Fracture clinic, outpatients, imaging, bone health and infection
question: What proportion of stable patients with suspected late or chronic fracture-related infection have at least 2 weeks off antibiotics before deep sampling?
why: An adequate antibiotic-free window before sampling is essential for accurate microbiology in chronic fracture-related infection, but this specific BOAST timing element is not covered by the library's existing FRI sampling audit [ONA-141], which measures the number of samples taken, not the antibiotic-free window beforehand.

standard.source: BOAST Fracture Related Infections (September 2019), standard 4E
standard.wording: For stable patients the optimum antibiotic free duration before sampling should be discussed with microbiology. In non-acute infections this should be a minimum of 2 weeks.

population: Inclusion: clinically stable adults having planned deep sampling (biopsy or debridement) for suspected late or chronic fracture-related infection, over the last 12 months. Exclusion: acutely septic patients needing emergency surgery.
sample: 20-30 consecutive planned sampling episodes for suspected late/chronic FRI over the last 12 months.
data_source: Medicines reconciliation/GP record, microbiology request form, pre-operative clinic letter, operation note.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'last antibiotic dose' and 'planned sampling date' field to the FRI clinic booking process, with a GP letter template asking GPs not to prescribe antibiotics for the wound in the 2 weeks before the planned date.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the orthopaedic infection governance meeting; if the GP letter and booking field reduce premature antibiotic exposure, embed both in the standard FRI work-up pathway.
evidence: No audit of the 2-week antibiotic-free sampling window for fracture-related infection exists in the library; [ONA-141] audits the number of samples taken, not this preceding step.
pitfalls: Patients may receive antibiotics from a GP or walk-in centre unknown to the orthopaedic team → check the GP record or ask the patient directly at every case.
Genuine systemic sepsis overrides the antibiotic-free window and should be excluded, not counted as a fail → apply the exclusion consistently.
A rigid 2-week rule can delay urgent surgical decision-making → record and discuss cases where microbiology explicitly agreed a shorter window as a pass, not a fail.
Patients may not disclose over-the-counter or dental antibiotic courses → ask specifically about any antibiotics, not only prescribed ones.
pearls: Recruit a consultant microbiologist to help define 'stable' and agree the GP letter wording.
Send the GP letter as soon as the sampling date is booked, not on the day of admission.
Use the same case list as the weekly bone and joint infection MDT audit to reduce duplicate data collection.
Keep the GP letter template live in the EPR discharge/clinic letter library after the audit team rotates.
effort: ~15 min per case from the GP record and clinic letters
pass: The patient has no antibiotics (prescribed or self-reported, including from the GP) for at least 2 weeks before deep sampling for suspected late or chronic FRI, or a documented microbiology discussion justifies a shorter window.

area: Fracture clinic, outpatients, imaging, bone health and infection
question: What proportion of adults having further surgery for a non-union or delayed union have microbiology and histology samples taken to exclude infection?
why: The BOAST FRI standard requires the same sampling work-up at secondary fracture surgery (for non-union or delayed union) as at initial suspected infection, but the library's existing sampling audit [ONA-141] is written for debridement or revision surgery for suspected infection, not for the wider population having non-union surgery where infection has not yet been suspected clinically.

standard.source: BOAST Fracture Related Infections (September 2019), standard 6
standard.wording: The presence of infection should be considered in any patient having further surgery following initial fracture fixation for instance for non or delayed union. ... Where surgical exposure allows, 5 samples for microbiology (using separate sterile instruments) and 2 for histology should be taken at the time of subsequent surgery unless the fracture is soundly united with no evidence for infection and the procedure was for the elective removal of metalwork.

population: Inclusion: adults having revision surgery for non-union or delayed union of a previously fixed fracture, over the last 6-12 months. Exclusion: elective metalwork removal in a soundly united, non-infected fracture (exception already defined in the standard).
sample: 30 consecutive non-union or delayed union revision operations over the last 6-12 months.
data_source: Operation note, microbiology and histology request/result system.

template.note: soundly united, no infection suspicion, elective metalwork removal

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add non-union and delayed union revision surgery to the same 'bone infection sampling kit' WHO sign-in prompt already used for suspected FRI debridements, so sampling becomes the default rather than something to remember separately.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the orthopaedic infection governance meeting; if extending the sampling kit prompt to this population works, keep it in the WHO sign-in permanently.
evidence: No audit of sampling at non-union/delayed union surgery exists in the library; [ONA-141] audits a narrower population already suspected of infection.
pitfalls: Surgeons may not consider infection likely in an apparently mechanical non-union, and skip sampling without documenting a reason → the standard asks infection to be 'considered' in every case, so absence of a documented decision should count as a fail.
Limited surgical exposure genuinely prevents full sampling in some cases → record this as a valid reason rather than a fail, but still count it in the denominator.
Confusing this audit with the existing FRI debridement sampling audit [ONA-141] risks double-counting patients → define the two populations clearly and keep them separate.
Histology turnaround delays can make results unavailable at the time of data collection → collect whether samples were sent, not just results.
pearls: Recruit the same infection MDT and theatre coordinator already engaged for [ONA-141]; the fix (a sampling kit) is shared.
Brief the trauma and limb reconstruction surgeons specifically, since non-union surgery is often booked as 'routine' rather than 'infection-related'.
Use real (anonymised) non-union cases in departmental teaching to show why sampling matters even without obvious infection signs.
Keep the extended WHO sign-in prompt live by updating the theatre checklist master copy, not a local printout.
effort: ~15 min per case from the operation note and lab system
pass: The operation note for non-union or delayed union surgery records 5 separate microbiology samples and 2 histology samples, or explicitly documents that the fracture was soundly united with no evidence of infection and the procedure was elective metalwork removal (an accepted exception).

area: Fracture clinic, outpatients, imaging, bone health and infection
question: What proportion of septic patients with suspected acute prosthetic joint infection have emergency surgical drainage within 6 hours?
why: The BOAST for acute PJI sets a 6-hour surgical target for the septic patient, distinct from the library's existing PJI audits [ONA-142, ONA-143], which cover antibiotic timing in non-septic patients and discharge information, not this emergency surgical standard.

standard.source: BOAST Acute Management of Peri-Prosthetic Joint Infection (October 2023), standard 3.3
standard.wording: requires emergent drainage and should have surgery performed by a suitably experienced surgical team as soon as is safe. In an acutely unwell patient this should be within 6 hours unless there are specific reasons that this is not possible.

population: Inclusion: adults presenting with sepsis and a suspected acute prosthetic joint infection, over the last 12-24 months. Exclusion: chronic, stable PJI without sepsis.
sample: 20-30 consecutive septic suspected acute PJI presentations over the last 12-24 months (this is a relatively rare emergency presentation, so a long window may be needed).
data_source: ED sepsis pathway documentation, theatre booking and start times, operation note.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect (extended window); Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-24 re-audit
change: Classify septic suspected acute PJI as an NCEPOD category 1 emergency on the theatre booking system, triggering immediate theatre and on-call consultant notification in the same way as other time-critical orthopaedic emergencies.
reaudit: At 12 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the orthopaedic infection governance and sepsis governance meetings; if the emergency booking category works, keep it as a standing theatre priority classification.
evidence: No audit of the 6-hour surgical standard for septic acute PJI exists in the library; [ONA-142] covers non-septic patients and [ONA-143] covers discharge information.
pitfalls: Case numbers will be small in any one hospital → pool data across a longer window or a network, and describe cases individually as well as in aggregate.
Competing theatre emergencies (e.g. open fractures, vascular injury) may delay this case legitimately → record competing cases as a documented reason, not a hidden delay.
Sepsis recognition time can be recorded inconsistently → use the time the 'sepsis six' pathway was started as the standard start point.
An unstable patient may need prolonged resuscitation before theatre is safe → this is a valid reason under the standard's own wording ('unless there are specific reasons'), so record it as such.
pearls: Recruit the sepsis lead and emergency theatre coordinator, since both pathways intersect in this standard.
Use the trust's existing sepsis-six audit process as an additional case-finding source.
Present timeline data (recognition, theatre booking, knife-to-skin) rather than a single figure, to show where any delay occurs.
Keep the NCEPOD category 1 classification live by adding it to the theatre booking system's fixed category list.
effort: ~20 min per case from ED, theatre and sepsis pathway records
pass: A septic patient with suspected acute PJI has surgical drainage started within 6 hours of the sepsis being recognised, or a documented specific reason explains a longer time.

area: Fracture clinic, outpatients, imaging, bone health and infection
question: What proportion of patients assessed for suspected prosthetic joint infection have a documented assessment for additional sources of infection, including endocarditis?
why: The BOAST PJI standard requires a general assessment for other infection sources including cardiovascular assessment for endocarditis as part of the comprehensive work-up, but this documentation item is not covered by the library's existing PJI audits [ONA-142, ONA-143, ONA-097], which focus on antibiotic timing and discharge advice.

standard.source: BOAST Acute Management of Peri-Prosthetic Joint Infection (October 2023), standard 5.2
standard.wording: a general assessment for additional sources of infection including a cardiovascular assessment for endocarditis.

population: Inclusion: adults assessed by orthopaedics for suspected acute prosthetic joint infection over the last 6 months. Exclusion: none.
sample: 30 consecutive suspected acute PJI assessments over the last 6 months.
data_source: Orthopaedic admission or clinic assessment note.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'other infection sources considered (including endocarditis)' field to the PJI assessment proforma, which cannot be left blank.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the orthopaedic infection governance meeting; if the mandatory field improves documentation, keep the proforma as the standard PJI assessment tool.
evidence: No audit of endocarditis/other-source assessment in suspected PJI exists in the library; other PJI audits [ONA-142, ONA-143, ONA-097] cover different standards.
pitfalls: Orthopaedic teams may feel this assessment 'belongs' to medicine or microbiology and skip it → the standard specifically asks for it as part of the orthopaedic comprehensive assessment, so frame the fix accordingly.
A brief 'no murmur' note may be too minimal to count as a considered assessment → agree what counts as adequate documentation before starting.
Bacteraemia results may arrive after the initial assessment, changing the risk → allow the field to be updated once culture results are known.
Overuse of echocardiography for every case would be inappropriate → the pass criterion is a documented assessment/comment, not routine echo for all.
pearls: Recruit a microbiologist or infectious diseases physician to help define what a 'considered' assessment looks like.
Combine data collection with the existing PJI antibiotic-timing audits [ONA-142] to reduce duplicate note review.
Use real case examples of bacteraemic PJI with missed endocarditis assessment (anonymised) to illustrate the stakes in teaching.
Keep the proforma field live by embedding it in the trust's standard PJI clerking template.
effort: ~10 min per case from the assessment note
pass: The orthopaedic assessment documents a general review for other infection sources and a specific comment on cardiovascular/endocarditis risk (murmur examination, relevant history, or echocardiogram request where indicated).

area: Fracture clinic, outpatients, imaging, bone health and infection
question: What proportion of patients assessed for suspected prosthetic joint infection have the full initial investigation panel of FBC, CRP, renal function and plain radiographs?
why: The BOAST PJI standard specifies a minimum initial investigation panel, but no audit in the library checks completeness of this basic work-up, as distinct from the antibiotic-timing and sampling standards already audited [ONA-142, ONA-097].

standard.source: BOAST Acute Management of Peri-Prosthetic Joint Infection (October 2023), standard 6
standard.wording: Initial investigations should include Full Blood Count, CRP, renal function, and plain radiographs.

population: Inclusion: adults presenting with suspected prosthetic joint infection over the last 3-6 months. Exclusion: none.
sample: 40 consecutive suspected PJI presentations over the last 3-6 months.
data_source: Laboratory results system, radiology system, admission/clinic assessment note.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Create a single 'suspected PJI' order set in the EPR that requests FBC, CRP, renal function and the appropriate plain radiograph together in one click.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the orthopaedic infection governance meeting; if the order set improves completeness, keep it as the default admission/clinic order set for suspected PJI.
evidence: No audit of initial investigation completeness for suspected PJI exists in the library; [ONA-142] and [ONA-097] audit antibiotic timing around sampling, not this initial panel.
pitfalls: A recent radiograph taken elsewhere (e.g. in clinic days earlier) may be wrongly excluded → allow any radiograph within a clinically reasonable window (e.g. 2 weeks) if repeat imaging is not indicated.
Renal function is often checked as part of a routine U&E and easy to miss counting → confirm creatinine/eGFR specifically, not just that 'bloods were sent'.
Out-of-hours presentations may have delayed radiograph access → record whether the delay was due to service availability.
The order set can become a 'tick box' exercise if results are not actioned → also check whether abnormal results changed management.
pearls: Recruit an ED and orthopaedic EPR administrator to build the order set quickly.
Pilot the order set in one clinical area (e.g. orthopaedic assessment unit) before wider rollout.
Reuse the same case list as the antibiotic-timing PJI audits [ONA-142] to minimise duplicate note review.
Keep the order set live by adding it to the EPR's standard order set library, not a personal favourite list.
effort: ~10 min per case from the lab and radiology systems
pass: All four investigations (FBC, CRP, renal function, plain radiographs of the affected joint) are requested and resulted within 24 hours of the suspected PJI assessment.

area: Orthopaedic perioperative, theatre and ward care
question: What proportion of elective orthopaedic operations use reusable (laundered) surgical gowns and drapes instead of single-use disposable ones?
why: The Intercollegiate Green Theatre Checklist recommends reusable textiles to cut theatre carbon footprint and waste, but the library's existing sustainability audits [ONA-122, ONA-123, ONA-150, ONA-151] cover catheters, histology, waste streams and instrument tray overage, not gown and drape choice.

standard.source: Intercollegiate Green Theatre Checklist v2.0 (November 2024), item 6
standard.wording: Evaluate PPE and sterile field requirements: rationalise use of non-sterile single-use gloves and PPE and opt for reusables when possible; limit sterile field to necessary areas only. Ensure availability of reusable textiles, including theatre hats, sterile gowns, patient drapes, and trolley covers.

population: Inclusion: all elective primary hip and knee replacement operations over the last 4-6 weeks. Exclusion: revision arthroplasty and cases with a documented high infection-risk reason for single-use gowns.
sample: 40 consecutive elective primary hip and knee replacement operations over the last 4-6 weeks.
data_source: Theatre stock/pick-list records, direct observation of gowns opened for the case, operation note.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Agree a written default of reusable gowns for routine elective primary arthroplasty with theatre sterile services, and remove single-use gowns from the default arthroplasty pick list so they must be actively requested.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the theatre sustainability and green theatre governance meeting; if the default pick-list change works, keep reusable gowns as the standard stock item for elective arthroplasty.
evidence: No audit of reusable versus single-use gown use exists in the library; existing green theatre audits [ONA-122, ONA-123, ONA-150, ONA-151] cover different checklist items.
pitfalls: Infection prevention teams may have local policies favouring single-use gowns for specific high-risk procedures → agree the exceptions list with infection control before starting.
Laundry turnaround and stock levels of reusable gowns can limit availability → check supply chain capacity before setting the pick-list default.
Staff comfort and familiarity with disposable gowns can drive continued use even when reusables are stocked → include staff feedback alongside the audit numbers.

Cost and carbon savings depend on genuine laundry-cycle data, which this audit does not itself measure → note this is a process audit, and pair it with the trust's sustainability team's carbon data if available.
pearls: Recruit the theatre sterile services manager and the trust's sustainability/green theatre lead as co-leads.
Use the Intercollegiate Green Theatre Checklist itself as a ready-made teaching resource for theatre staff.
Present the change alongside cost data (reusable gowns are typically cheaper over their laundry lifecycle), which helps engagement.
Keep the pick-list default live by updating theatre stores' master pick-list, not a temporary note.
effort: ~10 min per case from direct observation or the pick-list record
pass: The case uses reusable (laundered, non-disposable) surgical gowns for the scrub team, or a documented clinical reason (e.g. high fluid-risk procedure per local infection control policy) justifies single-use gowns.

area: Orthopaedic perioperative, theatre and ward care
question: What proportion of orthopaedic general anaesthetics using a volatile agent are given using low-flow (end-tidal controlled) anaesthesia?
why: Volatile anaesthetic gases are a major contributor to theatre carbon footprint, and low-flow anaesthesia substantially reduces this; the library's sustainability audits do not yet cover anaesthetic gas delivery.

standard.source: Intercollegiate Green Theatre Checklist v2.0 (November 2024), item 3
standard.wording: If using inhalational anaesthesia: use low-flow anaesthesia (via end-tidal anaesthetic gas control, if available).

population: Inclusion: all adults having a general anaesthetic with a volatile agent for elective orthopaedic surgery over the last 4-6 weeks. Exclusion: cases using total intravenous anaesthesia only, cases with a documented clinical reason for high flow (e.g. malignant hyperthermia risk).
sample: 40 consecutive volatile general anaesthetics for elective orthopaedic surgery over the last 4-6 weeks.
data_source: Anaesthetic e-record or paper anaesthetic chart (fresh gas flow rate over time).
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Set low-flow anaesthesia as the default target on the anaesthetic machine's electronic workflow prompt, with a reminder to reduce fresh gas flow once the patient is stable, agreed with the anaesthetic department.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the anaesthetic department and theatre sustainability meeting; if the workflow prompt increases low-flow use, keep it as a standard machine setting.
evidence: No audit of low-flow anaesthesia use in orthopaedic theatres exists in the library.
pitfalls: Not all anaesthetic machines have end-tidal gas control, limiting how low flow can safely go → record equipment availability alongside the result.
Induction and early maintenance legitimately need higher flow → measure low-flow achievement after the first few minutes of stable anaesthesia, not from time zero.
Anaesthetists may have individual practice preferences → present data anonymised by list rather than by named anaesthetist initially.
Desflurane has a far higher carbon impact than other volatiles regardless of flow rate → consider recording which agent was used as well as the flow rate.
pearls: Recruit an anaesthetic sustainability champion (many departments already have one) as co-lead.
Use the Intercollegiate Green Theatre Checklist's own compendium of evidence to support the teaching session.
Track total volatile agent usage (bottles used) as a simple parallel metric that is easy to trend over time.
Keep the practice alive by including it in anaesthetic departmental induction for new starters.
effort: ~10 min per case from the anaesthetic record
pass: The anaesthetic record shows fresh gas flow reduced to low-flow (typically ≤1 L/min) once the patient is stable, using end-tidal anaesthetic gas control where available.

area: Orthopaedic perioperative, theatre and ward care
question: What proportion of elective hip and knee replacement wounds are closed with sutures rather than metal staples?
why: The Green Theatre Checklist names suture skin closure as a lower-carbon alternative to staples, and sutures have a comparable or better evidence base for wound complications; the library has no audit of skin closure method choice.

standard.source: Intercollegiate Green Theatre Checklist v2.0 (November 2024), item 12
standard.wording: REPLACE: switch to low carbon alternatives (e.g. skin sutures vs. clips, "loose" antiseptic solutions in reusable gallipots).

population: Inclusion: all adults having primary elective hip or knee replacement over the last 4-6 weeks. Exclusion: revision arthroplasty, documented wound-specific reasons for staples (e.g. very thin or friable skin).
sample: 40 consecutive elective primary hip and knee replacements over the last 4-6 weeks.
data_source: Operation note, theatre stock/pick-list record.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Agree a written default of suture skin closure for routine primary elective arthroplasty with the arthroplasty surgeons, and set the theatre pick-list default to sutures, with staples available on specific request.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the theatre sustainability and arthroplasty governance meeting; if the default change is adopted and wound complication rates remain acceptable, keep sutures as the standard pick-list default.
evidence: No audit of skin closure method choice for sustainability exists in the library.
pitfalls: Surgeon preference and training background strongly influence closure method → present the evidence base (equivalent or better wound outcomes with sutures) alongside the audit to support a practice change conversation.
Wound closure time may increase slightly with sutures → consider recording closure time to address concerns directly.
A subset of patients (e.g. very thin skin, high tension closure) genuinely need staples → keep the exception category open and reviewed regularly.
This audit alone does not measure wound complication rates → pair it with existing surgical site infection surveillance data before making the change permanent.
pearls: Recruit an arthroplasty lead surgeon who already prefers sutures to champion the change with colleagues.
Present carbon and cost savings data together, since staples are also typically more expensive per case.
Check surgical site infection surveillance data at re-audit to reassure colleagues the change is safe.
Keep the pick-list default live by updating theatre stores' master list, not a temporary request.
effort: ~10 min per case from the operation note and pick-list record
pass: The skin is closed with sutures (not metal staples/clips) for a routine primary elective hip or knee replacement, or a documented clinical reason justifies staples.

question: What proportion of new orthopaedic referrals for tennis elbow have avoided a corticosteroid injection beforehand?
why: National guidance strongly advises against corticosteroid injection for lateral elbow tendinopathy because of worse medium-term outcomes, but the library has no elbow-specific audit at all; tennis elbow is one of the highest-volume upper limb soft-tissue referrals.

standard.source: BESS patient care pathway: Tennis elbow (Shoulder & Elbow 2023;15(4):348-359), summary of recommendations
standard.wording: Corticosteroid injection should not be used in the treatment of LET [lateral elbow tendinopathy] - Strong recommendation.

population: Inclusion: all adults referred to orthopaedics or a musculoskeletal service with a working diagnosis of tennis elbow (lateral elbow tendinopathy) over the last 6 months. Exclusion: referrals for red-flag features (fracture, dislocation, tumour, inflammatory arthritis).
sample: 30-40 consecutive new tennis elbow referrals over the last 6 months.
data_source: GP referral letter, clinic letter, medicines record/GP summary.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Share the BESS tennis elbow pathway and a one-page 'do not inject' summary with local GP practices and the musculoskeletal triage service, so physiotherapy becomes the automatic first step instead of injection.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the primary-secondary care musculoskeletal interface meeting; if referral patterns improve, add the pathway to the local GP referral guidance system permanently.
evidence: No audit of tennis elbow management exists in the library; there is no dedicated elbow audit topic in the corpus at all.
pitfalls: GPs may have already tried an injection years earlier for a different episode → ask specifically about the current episode.
Patients may have received an injection privately or from a physiotherapist without GP record → ask the patient directly as well as checking records.
Injection use may reflect limited access to physiotherapy rather than clinician choice → capture physiotherapy access/waiting time as context.
This is a primary-care-facing change, so orthopaedic teams alone cannot fix it → engage the musculoskeletal triage service and GP education leads directly.
pearls: Recruit a GP or musculoskeletal triage clinician as co-lead, since most of the change happens before referral.
Use the BESS pathway flowchart directly as an education resource for referrers.
Present the evidence (injections reversing to worse outcomes than placebo by 6 months) clearly, as this often changes practice quickly once seen.
Keep the pathway visible by adding it to the CCG/ICB musculoskeletal referral guidance, not just a one-off email.
effort: ~10 min per case from the referral letter and GP summary
pass: The patient has not received a corticosteroid injection for lateral elbow pain in primary or secondary care before or during their orthopaedic/physiotherapy assessment.

question: What proportion of adults with a straightforward clinical diagnosis of tennis elbow avoid unnecessary imaging before physiotherapy?
why: National guidance states plain radiographs are not essential and specialist imaging is not needed for treatment when the diagnosis is clinically clear, but no audit of imaging stewardship for this very common presentation exists in the library.

standard.source: BESS patient care pathway: Tennis elbow (Shoulder & Elbow 2023;15(4):348-359), Primary care/community triage services section
standard.wording: Plain radiographs of the elbow are not essential for confirming the diagnosis. Specialist imaging such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or computed tomography (CT) scans are not needed for treatment of LET in the primary care setting.

population: Inclusion: adults with a new clinical diagnosis of tennis elbow (insidious onset lateral elbow pain, tenderness over the lateral epicondyle, no history of trauma) seen in primary care or musculoskeletal triage over the last 6 months. Exclusion: any red-flag feature present.
sample: 30-40 consecutive new tennis elbow presentations over the last 6 months.
data_source: GP or musculoskeletal triage clinical record, radiology request system.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add the BESS diagnostic checklist to the musculoskeletal triage and GP referral template so imaging is only requested when a red-flag feature or diagnostic uncertainty is specifically documented.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the primary-secondary care musculoskeletal interface meeting and radiology demand management meeting; if the checklist reduces unnecessary imaging, embed it in the referral template permanently.
evidence: No audit of imaging stewardship for tennis elbow exists in the library; there is no dedicated elbow audit topic in the corpus at all.
pitfalls: Clinicians may request imaging for reassurance or because a patient asks for it → the fix should include clear patient-facing information explaining why imaging is not needed.
Genuine diagnostic uncertainty (e.g. in an older patient or atypical presentation) is a valid reason for imaging → record this as an exception, not a fail.
