Imaging requested for a different reason (e.g. incidental) should not be counted against this standard → check the stated indication on the request.
This crosses primary and secondary care, so a purely hospital-based fix will not reach GP-ordered imaging → involve the musculoskeletal triage/referral pathway directly.
pearls: Recruit a GP or musculoskeletal triage clinician as co-lead, since most imaging requests originate in primary care.
Use the BESS diagnostic flowchart as a simple, shareable one-page resource for referrers.
Present imaging cost and waiting-list impact data alongside the guideline evidence to strengthen the case for change.
Keep the checklist current by embedding it in the CCG/ICB musculoskeletal referral guidance, not a one-off circulation.
effort: ~10 min per case from the referral and radiology systems
pass: No X-ray, ultrasound, CT or MRI of the elbow is requested before a trial of physiotherapy, in a patient with a clinically clear diagnosis of tennis elbow and no red-flag features (trauma, swelling/lump, multi-joint involvement, suspected malignancy).

question: What proportion of patients aged 40 to 60 with a first traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation have rotator cuff imaging (ultrasound or MRI)?
why: Up to 40% of patients in this age group have a clinically relevant rotator cuff tear after dislocation, which is easily missed if imaging is not routinely considered; the library's only shoulder dislocation audit [ONA-156] covers post-reduction axillary nerve function, not rotator cuff assessment.

standard.source: BESS/BOA Patient Care Pathway: Traumatic anterior shoulder instability (Shoulder & Elbow 2015;7(3):214-226)
standard.wording: Patients between the ages of 40 years and 60 years have an increased risk of clinically relevant rotator cuff tears (approximately 40%) and, consequently should undergo routine ultrasound/magnetic resonance imaging to assess cuff integrity.

population: Inclusion: adults aged 40-60 with a first traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation, over the last 12 months. Exclusion: dislocation in the context of a known chronic cuff tear, atraumatic or recurrent dislocation.
sample: 30 consecutive eligible patients over the last 12 months.
data_source: ED/fracture clinic record, radiology request system, clinic letter.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic 'age 40-60: request shoulder ultrasound for cuff integrity' prompt to the fracture clinic outcome form whenever a first traumatic anterior dislocation is coded in this age group.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the shoulder/upper limb MDT and fracture clinic governance meeting; if the prompt increases appropriate imaging, keep it in the outcome form permanently.
evidence: No audit of rotator cuff imaging after shoulder dislocation exists in the library; [ONA-156] covers axillary nerve function, a different clinical question.
pitfalls: Cuff weakness can be masked by pain in the acute setting → the standard specifically recommends routine imaging for this age group rather than relying on examination alone, so imaging should not be skipped just because examination seemed normal.
Some patients recover full strength quickly and imaging may be deferred to a follow-up appointment → record whether imaging was requested at any point in the pathway, not only at first presentation.
Asymptomatic degenerative cuff tears are common with age and can confuse interpretation → this audit measures whether imaging was requested, not the clinical significance of any finding.
Patients may not attend for outpatient imaging after discharge from ED → track requests through to completion, not just the request being made.
pearls: Recruit the shoulder/upper limb clinical lead to define the exact age band and imaging pathway locally.
Use the fracture clinic outcome form as the single trigger point so the prompt reaches every relevant patient.
Present findings alongside any known missed rotator cuff tear cases to illustrate the clinical stakes.
Keep the prompt live by embedding it in the fracture clinic's standard outcome form, not a separate checklist.
effort: ~10 min per case from the clinic and radiology systems
pass: An ultrasound or MRI scan of the shoulder to assess rotator cuff integrity is requested within 6 weeks of a first traumatic anterior dislocation in a patient aged 40 to 60.

question: What proportion of shoulder dislocations have a documented neurological and circulatory examination before reduction?
why: Pre-reduction neurovascular assessment is essential for clinical and medico-legal reasons and to distinguish pre-existing nerve injury from a reduction complication; the library's only shoulder dislocation audit [ONA-156] covers documentation after reduction, not before.

standard.source: BESS/BOA Patient Care Pathway: Traumatic anterior shoulder instability (Shoulder & Elbow 2015;7(3):214-226)
standard.wording: It is essential, for clinical and medico-legal reasons, that a detailed and documented neurological (and circulatory) examination is performed prior to shoulder relocation.

population: Inclusion: all patients with a shoulder dislocation undergoing reduction in the emergency department over the last 3 months. Exclusion: none.
sample: 40 consecutive shoulder dislocation reductions over the last 3-6 months.
data_source: ED procedure note or shoulder reduction proforma.

template.note: for comparison with existing post-reduction audit

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory pre-reduction neurovascular examination box (paired with the existing post-reduction box) to the ED shoulder reduction procedure note, so the note cannot be completed without both.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the ED and trauma governance meeting; if the paired pre- and post-reduction box improves documentation, keep it in the standard procedure note template.
evidence: No audit of pre-reduction neurovascular documentation for shoulder dislocation exists in the library; the existing audit [ONA-156] covers only the post-reduction examination.
pitfalls: In a very painful, acute presentation, clinicians may examine but not document fully before moving quickly to reduce the joint → the fix should make documentation as quick as ticking a box, not writing free text.

Distinguishing pre-existing nerve injury from a reduction complication is only possible if the pre-reduction exam is genuinely done before, not after, reduction → clarify timing in the proforma design.
Sedation given before examination could affect the reliability of sensory testing → note whether sedation preceded the neuro exam.
This audit pairs naturally with the existing post-reduction audit [ONA-156]; running them together avoids duplicate note review but keep the two standards and pass criteria distinct in reporting.
pearls: Recruit an ED consultant with an interest in procedural sedation, since reduction technique and documentation are closely linked.
Combine data collection with the existing post-reduction audit [ONA-156] for efficiency, using one combined proforma covering both time points.
Use a simple diagram-based proforma (regimental badge area, deltoid, pulses) rather than free text to speed up completion.
Keep the paired box live by building it into the ED's electronic procedure note template.
effort: ~10 min per case from the ED procedure note
pass: A documented neurological examination (including axillary nerve sensation and deltoid function) and a circulatory examination (distal pulse) are recorded before the reduction attempt.

area: Fracture clinic, outpatients, imaging, bone health and infection
question: What proportion of new fracture clinic patients who need information in a different language or an accessible format have this recorded as provided?
why: National BOAST standards require accessible-format and language-appropriate information for fracture patients, but no audit in the library checks whether patients with a communication or language need actually receive it, an equity gap not covered by the library's plain-English letter audit [ONA-135].

standard.source: BOASt Outpatient and on-call services for people with fractures or musculoskeletal injury (BOA, February 2026), standard 7
standard.wording: Information in an accessible format and language should be available and include instructions for casts, splints, slings, and appliances.

population: Inclusion: new fracture clinic patients with a recorded communication or language need (interpreter required, learning disability, visual or hearing impairment) over the last 3-6 months. Exclusion: patients with no recorded communication need.
sample: 30 consecutive fracture clinic patients with a recorded communication or language need over the last 3-6 months (identify via PAS communication-needs flags or interpreter bookings).
data_source: PAS communication needs/flag field, interpreter booking system, clinic letter, plaster room record.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory check at fracture clinic booking that reads the PAS communication-needs flag and automatically books an interpreter or flags the need for an accessible-format information leaflet before the appointment.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the fracture clinic governance and trust equality/health inequalities meeting; if the automatic booking check works, keep it as the standard fracture clinic booking process.
evidence: No audit of accessible-format/language provision in fracture clinic exists in the library; [ONA-135] audits plain-English reading level of letters for the general population, a different equity dimension.
pitfalls: Communication needs may not be recorded accurately or consistently on PAS → cross-check with ward or ED records where possible and report the recording gap itself as a finding.
An interpreter booked but not attending on the day is a common real-world failure → record actual use, not just booking.
Family members are sometimes used informally as interpreters, which is not equivalent to a professional interpreter → record this separately and do not count it as a pass.
Small numbers of patients with each type of need make percentages unstable → report by need category as well as combined.
pearls: Recruit the trust's interpreting and translation service manager as co-lead.
Use the trust's equality, diversity and inclusion or health inequalities lead to help frame and present the findings.
Pilot the automatic booking check in one fracture clinic before wider rollout.
Keep the check live by embedding it in the booking team's standard operating procedure, not an individual's reminder.
effort: ~15 min per case from PAS, interpreter booking and clinic records
pass: A patient recorded as needing a language interpreter, an easy-read format, or another accessible communication format has this need documented and the corresponding format/interpreter actually used or arranged for their fracture clinic information.

area: Fracture clinic, outpatients, imaging, bone health and infection
question: What proportion of patients with a first-time lateral patellar dislocation are assessed by a musculoskeletal physiotherapist within 3 weeks of injury?
why: The national FTLPD standard sets a specific early physiotherapy assessment target that is distinct from, and not covered by, the library's existing patellar dislocation audit [ONA-166], which measures only the skyline X-ray view.

standard.source: BOA Standard: Assessment and Management of First Time Lateral Patellar Dislocation (FTLPD) (December 2024), standard 8
standard.wording: Assessment by a musculo-skeletal physiotherapist should occur within 3 weeks of injury.

population: Inclusion: all patients (any age) with a first-time lateral patellar dislocation managed non-operatively as the initial plan, over the last 6 months. Exclusion: patients proceeding directly to surgery for an associated injury before physiotherapy would be due.
sample: 30-40 consecutive first-time lateral patellar dislocations over the last 6 months.
data_source: ED/fracture clinic record, physiotherapy referral and appointment system.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a direct physiotherapy self-referral or fast-track booking option to the virtual fracture clinic outcome form for first-time patellar dislocation, bypassing the general physiotherapy waiting list.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the knee/sports injury MDT and physiotherapy service governance meeting; if the fast-track referral works, keep it as the standard pathway for this diagnosis.
evidence: No audit of the BOA FTLPD physiotherapy timing standard exists in the library; the existing audit [ONA-166] covers a different standard (skyline X-ray view) from the same guideline.
pitfalls: General physiotherapy waiting lists may make the 3-week target unachievable without a dedicated pathway → escalate capacity constraints if the fast-track referral does not resolve the gap.
Patients may be referred but not attend their first appointment → record both referral date and actual attendance date.
Diagnosis coding for 'patellar dislocation' can be inconsistent between ED and fracture clinic systems → cross-check both sources when identifying cases.
A patient who self-refers to a private physiotherapist would still meet the clinical intent but may not appear in hospital data → note this as a data limitation.
pearls: Recruit the musculoskeletal physiotherapy service lead as co-lead, since capacity is the likely rate-limiting step.
Use the same case list as any recurrent patellar instability MRI audit already running, since patients may overlap.
Agree the fast-track referral criteria and capacity with physiotherapy before cycle 1, not after finding a gap.
Keep the fast-track pathway live by adding it to the virtual fracture clinic outcome form permanently.
effort: ~10 min per case from the fracture clinic and physiotherapy systems
pass: The patient is seen by a musculoskeletal physiotherapist within 3 weeks (21 days) of the date of dislocation.

area: Fracture clinic, outpatients, imaging, bone health and infection
question: What proportion of patients considered for surgery after a first-time lateral patellar dislocation have this discussed and documented at an age-appropriate MDT?
why: The national FTLPD standard requires MDT or peer-review discussion before surgery is offered, to avoid unnecessary stabilisation procedures; this specific governance step is not covered by the library's existing patellar dislocation audit [ONA-166].

standard.source: BOA Standard: Assessment and Management of First Time Lateral Patellar Dislocation (FTLPD) (December 2024), standard 13
standard.wording: Clinicians considering surgery following FTLPD should discuss their plan within an age-appropriate multi-disciplinary team meeting, or alternative forum for peer review, with written documentation of the outcome included in the medical records.

population: Inclusion: all patients considered for surgery (for the dislocation itself or an associated injury) after a first-time lateral patellar dislocation, over the last 12 months. Exclusion: emergency surgery for an acute vascular or open injury.
sample: 20-30 consecutive patients considered for surgery after FTLPD over the last 12 months.
data_source: MDT/peer-review meeting minutes, clinic letter, theatre listing form.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add 'FTLPD surgical plan' as a standing agenda item template in the knee/sports injury or paediatric orthopaedic MDT, with a mandatory outcome-recording field linked to the theatre listing form.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the knee/sports injury and paediatric orthopaedic MDT governance meeting; if the standing agenda item works, keep it as a permanent MDT process.
evidence: No audit of MDT discussion before FTLPD surgery exists in the library; the existing audit [ONA-166] covers a different standard (skyline X-ray view) from the same guideline.
pitfalls: A single-surgeon department may not have a formal MDT and rely on informal peer discussion → the standard allows an 'alternative forum for peer review', so define and document what this looks like locally.
Surgery decided in a busy clinic without a documented discussion is easy to miss from case-finding → cross-check theatre listing forms against MDT minutes systematically.
Skeletally immature patients may go through a different (paediatric) MDT to adults → make sure both age-appropriate forums are captured.
Retrospective documentation of an MDT outcome after the decision was already made in clinic would not meet the spirit of the standard → check the dates are in the correct order.
pearls: Recruit both adult knee/sports injury and paediatric orthopaedic leads, since the standard applies across ages.
Use the recurrent patellar instability assessment standard's own MRI findings as part of the MDT discussion template.
Agree what counts as an acceptable 'alternative forum for peer review' locally before cycle 1.
Keep the agenda item live by giving the MDT coordinator ownership of the standing template.
effort: ~10 min per case from MDT minutes and the listing form
pass: The decision to offer surgery after a first-time lateral patellar dislocation is documented as having been discussed at an age-appropriate MDT or peer-review forum before listing.

area: Foot and ankle, hand and wrist, spine
question: What proportion of adults with non-specific low back pain (with or without sciatica) in a non-specialist setting avoid routine spinal imaging?
why: Unnecessary lumbar spine imaging drives further unhelpful investigation and patient anxiety without changing management; the library's spine audits focus heavily on cauda equina and traumatic fracture imaging, with no audit of this very high-volume imaging stewardship standard.

standard.source: NICE NG59 rec 1.1.4 (2016)
standard.wording: Do not routinely offer imaging in a non-specialist setting for people with low back pain with or without sciatica. [2016]

population: Inclusion: adults presenting to primary care or a non-specialist musculoskeletal/orthopaedic triage service with low back pain, with or without sciatica, over the last 3 months. Exclusion: any red-flag feature present (cauda equina symptoms, unexplained weight loss, history of cancer, significant trauma, fever, progressive neurological deficit).
sample: 40 consecutive eligible low back pain presentations over the last 3 months.
data_source: GP or musculoskeletal triage clinical record, radiology request system.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory red-flag checklist to the GP and musculoskeletal triage low back pain template that must be completed before an imaging request can be submitted for non-specific low back pain.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the primary care and musculoskeletal interface meeting and radiology demand management meeting; if the checklist reduces unnecessary imaging, embed it in the referral/request system permanently.
evidence: No audit of imaging stewardship for non-specific low back pain exists in the library; existing spine audits cover cauda equina and traumatic fracture imaging, a different population.
pitfalls: Patient expectation and anxiety commonly drive imaging requests → pair the checklist with patient-facing information explaining why imaging is not needed without red flags.
Clinicians may document a red flag loosely to justify imaging they already intended to request → define red flags precisely in the checklist to reduce this.
Imaging requested by a specialist (e.g. after referral) is outside the scope of this non-specialist-setting standard → clearly define the non-specialist population before starting.
This crosses primary and secondary care, so a hospital-only fix will not reach all GP-ordered imaging → involve GP practices or the musculoskeletal triage service directly.
pearls: Recruit a GP with a special interest in musculoskeletal medicine or the musculoskeletal triage lead as co-lead.
Use the existing NICE NG59 red-flag list as a ready-made teaching and checklist resource.
Present imaging cost and reporting turnaround data alongside the guideline evidence to strengthen engagement.
Keep the checklist current by embedding it in the CCG/ICB musculoskeletal referral and imaging request guidance.
effort: ~10 min per case from the clinical record and radiology system
pass: No lumbar spine X-ray, CT or MRI is requested in primary care or a non-specialist musculoskeletal clinic for a patient with non-specific low back pain (with or without sciatica) and no red-flag features.

question: What proportion of patients with a confirmed limb arterial injury from musculoskeletal trauma have revascularisation started within 1 hour of arrival?
why: Revascularisation is a time-critical (NCEPOD 1) emergency with no safe ischaemic time, and knee dislocation is a classic cause; the library's existing audit [ONA-034] measures pulse documentation in the ED but not the time to definitive treatment once an arterial injury is confirmed.

standard.source: BOA/BAPRAS/Vascular Society Standard: Diagnosis and management of arterial injuries associated with musculoskeletal trauma (June 2026), standard 10
standard.wording: Revascularisation is an emergency procedure (NCEPOD 1) and should be commenced within one hour of arrival to hospital.

population: Inclusion: patients with a confirmed arterial injury associated with musculoskeletal trauma (including knee dislocation, tibial plateau or distal femoral fracture with vascular compromise) over the last 12-24 months. Exclusion: supracondylar fractures in children (covered by a separate BOAST).
sample: 15-25 consecutive confirmed arterial injury cases over the last 12-24 months (this is a rare, high-harm emergency, so a long window and possibly network-level pooling is needed).
data_source: ED arrival time (trauma call record), theatre start time, operation note.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect (extended window); Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-24 re-audit
change: Classify confirmed limb arterial injury as an NCEPOD category 1 emergency on the theatre booking system with immediate simultaneous notification of orthopaedic, vascular or plastic surgery on-call teams, bypassing the standard trauma list queue.
reaudit: At 12 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the trauma network governance meeting and submit alongside TARN data; if the emergency booking classification reduces time to revascularisation, keep it as a standing theatre priority category.
evidence: No audit of the 1-hour revascularisation standard exists in the library; the related audit [ONA-034] measures ED pulse documentation, an earlier step in the same pathway.
pitfalls: Case numbers are small and high-stakes → review every case individually as well as in aggregate, and involve the trauma network mortality and morbidity process.
Time of injury versus time of arrival can be confused → the standard specifies time of arrival to hospital as the start point, so use that consistently.
Transfer from a non-specialist centre adds an unavoidable delay before the clock at the receiving centre starts → record transfer time separately from in-hospital delay.
Competing emergencies (e.g. major haemorrhage) may genuinely delay theatre access → record this as a documented reason, not a hidden delay.
pearls: Recruit vascular and plastic surgery colleagues as co-leads, since the standard requires consultant-led joint care.
Use the trauma network's existing arterial injury or limb trauma governance process as the case-finding route.
Present a timeline (arrival, CT angiogram, theatre start) for each case to show exactly where any delay occurs.
Keep the NCEPOD category 1 classification live by embedding it in the theatre booking system's fixed category list.
effort: ~20 min per case from ED, radiology and theatre records
pass: Surgical revascularisation is commenced within 1 hour of the patient's arrival at hospital.

question: What proportion of patients with suspected limb arterial injury have CT angiography performed concurrently with the initial trauma CT, rather than as a delayed second scan?
why: Performing CT angiography at the same time as the trauma CT avoids a second scan and the delay this causes to diagnosis and revascularisation; the library's existing audit [ONA-029] covers CT angiography for cervical spine injury specifically, not limb arterial injury.

standard.source: BOA/BAPRAS/Vascular Society Standard: Diagnosis and management of arterial injuries associated with musculoskeletal trauma (June 2026), standard 8
standard.wording: CT angiogram is recommended if arterial injury is suspected and should be performed concurrently with whole-body CT.

population: Inclusion: trauma patients with a suspected limb arterial injury (absent or asymmetric pulse after reduction and splinting) who proceed to CT, over the last 12 months. Exclusion: patients going directly to theatre without CT due to overwhelming clinical urgency.
sample: 20-30 consecutive suspected limb arterial injury CT episodes over the last 12 months.
data_source: Radiology information system (scan protocol and times), trauma CT report.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic CT angiography arterial-phase extension to the trauma CT protocol whenever 'suspected limb arterial injury' is selected on the trauma CT request, so radiographers do not need a separate request.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the trauma radiology governance meeting; if the combined protocol works, keep it as the default trauma CT protocol option.
evidence: No audit of concurrent CT angiography for suspected limb arterial injury exists in the library; the related audit [ONA-029] covers cervical spine injury, a different indication.
pitfalls: Radiographers may not always know a limb arterial injury is suspected at the time of the initial scan → make 'suspected arterial injury' a clear, separate tick box on the trauma CT request form.
Renal function may limit additional contrast in some patients → record any documented contrast-related reason for a separate or deferred scan.

A patient stabilised and reduced after the initial scan may develop new concern for arterial injury later → a later, separate CTA is appropriate in this scenario and should be recorded as a valid reason, not a fail.
Protocol changes need radiology and trauma team agreement together → involve both from the outset.
pearls: Recruit a trauma radiologist and radiographer superintendent as co-leads, since the protocol change is theirs to implement.
Use real (anonymised) cases where a second scan delayed revascularisation to illustrate the value of the change.
Combine data collection with the 1-hour revascularisation audit, since the same patients are involved.
Keep the protocol extension live by adding it to the trauma CT protocol library in the radiology system.
effort: ~10 min per case from the radiology system
pass: CT angiography of the affected limb is performed as part of the same CT episode as the initial trauma/whole-body CT, with no separate second scan visit required.

question: What proportion of adults with a 'possible target' meniscal lesion and symptoms under 3 months are offered a structured non-operative trial before arthroscopic surgery is considered?
why: The BASK meniscal guideline directs a first-line non-operative trial for possible-target lesions with short symptom duration, avoiding premature surgery; no audit in the library checks this specific staging step.

standard.source: BASK Arthroscopic Meniscal Surgery: A National Society Treatment Guideline and Consensus Statement (Bone Joint J 2019;101-B:652-659), Meniscal Tear Management Guideline flowchart
standard.wording: Possible Meniscal Target (MRI) & Corresponding Symptoms/Signs, Symptoms < 3 months: Assessment: Further non-surgical treatment is first line. Recommendation: Optimal Non-Operative Treatment & Re-assess (e.g. provide information, physiotherapy, exercise, analgesia, steroid injection).

population: Inclusion: adults with an MRI-reported 'possible target' meniscal lesion and symptom duration under 3 months, discussed in a knee clinic over the last 6-12 months. Exclusion: locked knee, clear 'target' lesion, symptoms of 3 months or more.
sample: 20-30 consecutive eligible knee clinic patients over the last 6-12 months.
data_source: MRI report, knee clinic letter, physiotherapy referral system.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 'possible target, symptoms <3 months: non-operative trial plan' prompt to the knee clinic letter template that must be completed before a surgical listing option becomes available for this category.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the knee/sports injury MDT; if the prompt reduces premature listing, keep it in the standard clinic letter template.
evidence: No audit of this BASK staging step exists in the library; other meniscal audits in this batch cover MRI confirmation and locked-knee timing, not this earlier decision point.
pitfalls: Classifying a lesion as 'target' versus 'possible target' relies on radiologist and surgeon agreement, which can vary → agree the definition locally using the BASK terminology before starting.
Patients may push for early surgery having researched their MRI report → record shared decision-making discussion as part of the non-operative pathway.
Symptom duration can be difficult to pin down precisely → use the patient's best estimate and record it consistently.
This can read as restricting surgeon autonomy → present it as following an agreed national consensus guideline, not local policy.
pearls: Recruit the knee/sports injury lead surgeon to define local application of the BASK terminology.
Reuse the same case list as the MRI confirmation and advanced-OA overuse audits in this batch to reduce duplicate note review.
Share the BASK flowchart directly with the surgical team as the source of authority for the fix.
Keep the clinic letter prompt live by embedding it in the standard knee clinic template.
effort: ~15 min per case from the MRI report and clinic letter
pass: A patient with a 'possible target' meniscal lesion on MRI and symptoms present for less than 3 months has a documented structured non-operative treatment plan (physiotherapy, exercise, analgesia or injection) before any arthroscopic listing.

question: What proportion of shoulder dislocations have two orthogonal radiographic views before reduction is attempted?
why: A single view can miss the direction of dislocation or an associated fracture, but no audit in the library checks pre-reduction imaging adequacy for shoulder dislocation; the existing audit [ONA-156] covers post-reduction nerve function only.

standard.source: BESS/BOA Patient Care Pathway: Traumatic anterior shoulder instability (Shoulder & Elbow 2015;7(3):214-226)
standard.wording: Two views are required to confirm glenohumeral dislocation and the direction of dislocation. An antero-posterior radiograph is obligatory. Ideally, an axial view should also be obtained as the second view.

population: Inclusion: all patients with a suspected or confirmed shoulder dislocation presenting to the emergency department over the last 3-6 months. Exclusion: none.
sample: 40 consecutive shoulder dislocation presentations over the last 3-6 months.
data_source: Radiology information system (views requested and performed), ED procedure note.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Set the default ED radiology request protocol for 'suspected shoulder dislocation' to always include both an AP and an axial (or modified axial) view as a single combined request.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the ED and radiology governance meeting; if the combined default request improves compliance, keep it as the standard shoulder dislocation imaging protocol.
evidence: No audit of pre-reduction imaging adequacy for shoulder dislocation exists in the library; [ONA-156] audits post-reduction nerve function, a different standard from the same guideline family.
pitfalls: Severe pain can genuinely prevent a second view being obtained before reduction → the guideline itself allows a modified axial or scapular Y view as an alternative, so record which alternative (if any) was used.
Clinicians experienced in recognising dislocation direction clinically may feel a second view is unnecessary → present the medico-legal and diagnostic value of confirming direction before reduction.
Radiographer availability out of hours can limit view choice → record time of day to see if this explains variation.
Recurrent dislocators with a well-documented pattern may reasonably need less imaging → consider excluding known recurrent dislocations with a typical re-presentation if locally agreed.
pearls: Recruit an ED radiographer lead to help set the default combined request protocol.
Combine data collection with the pre-reduction neurovascular examination audit in this batch, since the same patients and notes are involved.
Use example missed posterior dislocations (single-view AP only) in teaching to illustrate the risk.
Keep the combined request protocol live by adding it to the RIS default request set for this presentation.
effort: ~10 min per case from the radiology and ED systems
pass: An AP view plus an axial (or modified axial/scapular Y) second view are obtained before the reduction attempt, or a documented reason (e.g. pain precluding positioning) explains a single view with an accepted alternative technique.

question: What proportion of ACL reconstruction consent discussions document the graft options, risks and the surgeon's recommendation?
why: The BOA ACL standard requires graft selection (autograft, allograft, synthetic) with its benefits, complications and risks to be discussed and documented at consent; this specific consent element is not covered by any audit in the library.

standard.source: BOA Specialty Standard: Best Practice for Management of Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Injuries (September 2020), standard 7b
standard.wording: Graft selection should be discussed including autograft, allograft and synthetic ligaments. This should include the benefits, complications and risks of all and the preferred graft recommendation.

population: Inclusion: all adults consented for primary ACL reconstruction over the last 6 months. Exclusion: revision surgery where graft choice is highly constrained by prior surgery (record separately).
sample: 30-40 consecutive ACL reconstruction consent episodes over the last 6 months.
data_source: Consent form, pre-operative clinic letter.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a structured 'graft choice discussion' section to the ACL consent form or a paired patient information sheet, with tick boxes for each graft type discussed and a free-text line for the agreed choice.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the knee/sports injury MDT; if the structured section improves documentation, keep it as the standard ACL consent form.
evidence: No audit of ACL graft-choice consent documentation exists in the library.
pitfalls: Standard hospital consent forms often have very limited space for procedure-specific detail → use a paired information sheet if the consent form itself cannot be extended.
Patients may already have a strong graft preference from research beforehand → document this as part of the discussion, not a substitute for it.
Trainees consenting patients may be less confident discussing all graft options → pair the fix with a short teaching session on graft choice discussion.
A generic 'risks discussed' tick box without naming graft types would not meet the standard → the fix must specifically separate out graft-related discussion.
pearls: Recruit the knee/sports injury lead surgeon to draft the structured wording.
Use the existing National Ligament Registry consent audit in this batch as a combined data collection opportunity, since both relate to the same consent episode.
Give patients a copy of the graft-choice information sheet to take home, improving both consent quality and patient experience.
Keep the structured section live by embedding it in the standard ACL consent bundle.
effort: ~10 min per case from the consent form and clinic letter
pass: The consent form or pre-operative clinic letter documents the graft options considered, their benefits/risks, and the agreed graft choice.

question: What proportion of patients referred to secondary care for tennis elbow have a PRTEE (Patient-Rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation) score recorded before treatment starts?
why: The BESS tennis elbow pathway defines PRTEE as the core outcome measure for this condition, but the library has no audit of outcome measurement for any elbow condition, making it impossible to track whether treatment is working.

standard.source: BESS patient care pathway: Tennis elbow (Shoulder & Elbow 2023;15(4):348-359), Outcome metrics section
standard.wording: The core outcome set for LET defined by Bateman et al. PRTEE; PRTEE pain & function subscale.

population: Inclusion: adults newly referred to secondary care or a musculoskeletal service for tennis elbow (lateral elbow tendinopathy) over the last 6 months. Exclusion: red-flag referrals for an alternative diagnosis.
sample: 30 consecutive new tennis elbow secondary care assessments over the last 6 months.
data_source: Clinic letter, physiotherapy or orthopaedic assessment record, PROM collection system if one exists.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add the PRTEE questionnaire as a mandatory patient self-completed form in the waiting area at every new tennis elbow appointment, with the score entered into the clinic letter template.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the musculoskeletal/upper limb service governance meeting; if the self-completed form works, keep it as standard practice for every new tennis elbow assessment.
evidence: No audit of outcome measurement for any elbow condition exists in the library.
pitfalls: A new questionnaire adds to clinic administrative burden → keep it a short, patient-self-completed form to minimise staff time.
Patients with limited literacy or English as a second language may need support completing it → have an accessible-format or interpreter-assisted version available.
A score recorded but never reviewed at follow-up is of limited value → also check whether a repeat PRTEE is planned to track progress.
Digital and paper systems may both be in use locally, risking inconsistent recording → agree a single method before starting.
pearls: Recruit the musculoskeletal physiotherapy service, since they usually run outcome measure collection already for other conditions.
Use the BESS-defined PRTEE as the core outcome set, avoiding the need to develop a local measure.
Feed results back to referrers to demonstrate the value of the pathway.
Keep the form live by adding it to the department's standard new-patient paperwork pack.
effort: ~10 min per case; the PRTEE itself takes the patient under 5 minutes to complete
pass: A PRTEE score (or its pain and function subscales) is recorded at the first secondary care assessment before any new treatment is started.

area: Fracture clinic, outpatients, imaging, bone health and infection
question: What proportion of patients with a first-time lateral patellar dislocation are given patient information about their injury and rehabilitation?
why: The national FTLPD standard requires accessible patient information (leaflet, video or app-based) to be available, but the library's existing patellar dislocation audit [ONA-166] does not check this information-provision step.

standard.source: BOA Standard: Assessment and Management of First Time Lateral Patellar Dislocation (FTLPD) (December 2024), standard 15
standard.wording: Appropriate patient information including leaflets, videos or online / app-based content should be available.

population: Inclusion: all patients with a first-time lateral patellar dislocation assessed in ED or fracture clinic over the last 3-6 months. Exclusion: none.
sample: 40 consecutive first-time lateral patellar dislocation presentations over the last 3-6 months.
data_source: ED discharge record, fracture clinic letter, patient information leaflet log if one exists.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Create a single FTLPD patient information leaflet (with a QR code linking to a rehabilitation video) and add a mandatory 'information given: yes/no, format' field to the ED and fracture clinic discharge template for this diagnosis.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the knee/sports injury MDT and fracture clinic governance meeting; if the leaflet and mandatory field work, keep both as standard practice for this diagnosis.
evidence: No audit of patient information provision for FTLPD exists in the library; the existing audit [ONA-166] covers a different standard (skyline X-ray view) from the same guideline.
pitfalls: Verbal advice alone is easy to give but hard to verify or standardise → the fix should make written/digital information the default, with verbal advice as a supplement.
Information given in ED may not be repeated or reinforced at fracture clinic follow-up → check both points in the pathway.
A leaflet only in English may not meet the needs of all patients → pair this with the accessible-format/language audit in this batch where relevant.
Staff may forget to document that a leaflet was given even when it was → make documentation as quick as a single tick box.
pearls: Recruit the physiotherapy team to help create rehabilitation video content, since they already produce exercise materials.
Use the BOA standard itself as the justification when presenting the change to ED and fracture clinic staff.
Combine data collection with the physiotherapy-timing audit in this batch, since the same patients are involved.
Keep the leaflet current by giving the knee/sports injury service ownership of periodic review and updates.
effort: ~10 min per case from the ED and fracture clinic records
pass: The patient's record documents that written, video or app-based information about first-time patellar dislocation and its rehabilitation was given or signposted at the first assessment.
